newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF hopes to finish January review of Russia soon.
newsitem.headline: IMF hopes to finish January review of Russia soon.

text.p: IMF officials have almost finished a January review of the Russian economy, which will allow them to decide whether to pay out delayed instalments of a $10 billion loan, the IMF's Moscow representative said on Friday.
"I'm hoping that it may be completed by the end of today, although it could slip into the early part of next week. We're very close to the end," Tom Wolf told Reuters.
If the review is positive the International Monetary Fund board will meet roughly a week later to decide whether to disburse additional tranches of the three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF).
A fund mission left Moscow at the end of last week before completing all the work on the regular assessment, and local officials have been putting the final touches to it this week.

The IMF delayed several payments of the credit in the second half of last year because tax revenues were well below budgeted levels, threatening to undermine government finances, and because the government was slow to meet reform promises.
Russia agreed a programme of economic performance and structural reforms with the IMF as a condition for the loan.
Lending resumed at the end of 1996, but Russia has not yet received tranches for November and December, each worth around $330 million, and January's instalment is now also due.
Economists who follow the talks said the IMF's assessment was likely to be positive and the board could agree to pay out both the November and December tranches next month.
The IMF will be pleased by several structural reforms for which it has long been pushing.
Firstly the government is to rationalise natural gas charges to reflect transport costs.

The powerful gas monopoly Gazprom has been resisting government efforts to end its single national charge for gas, which meant some consumers were paying more than they should while others received gas below cost price.
Secondly the government is to cut the long list of strategic customers of utilities, who cannot be cut off even if they do not pay their bills.
This will help the utilities and benefit government revenues by cutting through part of the web of non-payments choking the Russian economy.
Lastly the government has dropped plans to impose a quota on vodka imports, and will instead license sales of vodka.
On the financial side, economists say there was a big improvement in tax revenues in December.
January is turning out to be a poor month, but that is partly due to seasonal factors, and economists said the overall fiscal trend was good.
An IMF mission will return to Moscow around February 12 for the next regular monthly assessment, and also to finish work on a detailed economic programme for the whole of 1997, Wolf said.

By then another precondition for payments of the loan this year should have been met, as the upper house of parliament will have had a chance to pass the 1997 budget, which has already been approved by the lower house.
